2.3.5 Operant conditioning 
(Charles & Jennifer, n.d.) describes operant conditioning as a theory within 
psychology where through the use of rewards, certain behaviours are reenforced 
or diminished.  
(Charles & Jennifer, n.d.) describes five methods: 
1. Positive reinforcement – Reward for successful actions or tasks 
completed; this could be done with scores or badges. 
2. Negative reinforcement – Removing undesirable elements; this might 
involve less lessons since a student may have mastered a topic. 
3. Positive punishment – Using undesirable actions to stop a certain trait, 
this might involve visibly reducing the score when a student gets a 
question wrong. 
4. Negative punishment – Removing a desirable element to stop a certain 
trait, an example might include resetting a streak, after a user fails to 
use the application within 24-hours. 
Operant conditioning offers a framework to reward or punish students to develop 
and grow desirable traits. 
2.3.6 Active Learning and Higher Order Cognitive Processing 
Active learning may offer insights into improving higher order thinking for a 
microlearning framework. With more traditional learning methods, students take 
a passive role within the classroom, resulting in them becoming less engaged 
(O’Neill & McMahon, 2005). On the other hand, active learning requires a 
student to think beyond just memorisation, and promotes them to think 
critically, explore and challenge their existing schemas (Petress, 2008).
